description: Before Zeus, his father Cronos devoured his children. This is how the void gave birth to the gods of Olympus.

hero.hook: Before Olympus, the world is born in emptiness, violence and family coups.

blocks.text: Before the gods of **Olympus** reigned, Greek mythology imagines an original void: **Chaos**. It's not a noisy mess. It is a gap, an abyss from which life emerges.

The birth of gods is not sweet. It is a series of crises and power grabs. The poet **Hesiod**, in the 8th century BCE, recounts it in the [[Hesiod's Theogony]]. This is how the world moves from the void to the court of **Zeus**.
From **Chaos** forces are first born without a human face. **Gaia**, Earth, provides solid ground. The **Tartar** is a prison deep beneath the world. **Eros**, desire, allows beings to unite.

blocks.caption: Gaia, the Earth, first power of the Greek world.

blocks.text: Gaia alone generates **Ouranos**, the Starry Sky. From their couple are born the **Titans**, gods of brute force, and monsters: the **Cyclops** and the **Hecatonchires**, giants with a hundred arms.
For the Greeks, the world does not arise from nothing. It is born from a separation: the space between Heaven and Earth finally gives way to life.
Ouranos hates his children. He locks them in Gaia's womb. The Earth is suffocating. The first revolution of the cosmos is preparing.

sections.title: From Chaos are born Earth and Sky

blocks.text: Gaia forges a sickle from [[adamant]], a legendary metal of absolute hardness. Only the youngest Titan, the cunning **Kronos**, agrees to act. Hidden in his mother's side, he castrates Ouranos and separates Heaven from Earth forever.
Kronos becomes king. But the blood of Ouranos still fertilizes the world: the **Érinyes**, goddesses of family vengeance, and **Aphrodite**, goddess of love, emerged from the sea foam.
The name **Aphrodite** comes from the Greek “aphros”, “foam”. His birth recalls the crime which opened the reign of Cronus.

A prophecy threatens Cronus: one of his sons will dethrone him. To avoid it, he devours his children as soon as they are born, **Hestia**, **Demeter**, **Hera**, **Hades**, **Poseidon**. The Greek gods have very human fears: it's the [[Greek divine anthropomorphism]].

**Rhea**, wife of Kronos, refuses to lose her last child. She hands him a swaddled stone. The real baby, **Zeus**, grows up in secret in the [[Dicté]] cave in Crete. The [[Courètes]], sacred warriors, cover his tears with their cries. The goat **Amalthée** feeds him.

As an adult, Zeus forces Cronus to regurgitate his siblings. The children come out ready to fight. The **Titanomachy** begins, a ten-year war between Titans and future Olympians. The Cyclops offer Zeus the decisive weapon: the **lightning**.

blocks.text: The Titans are thrown into Tartarus. **Zeus** takes the Sky, **Poseidon** the seas, **Hades** the world of the dead. The **Olympus** becomes a divine court, more orderly than the force of the Titans.

sections.title: Zeus frees his brothers and sisters

blocks.text: Even victorious, Zeus remains worried. He marries **Métis**, Wisdom, then swallows her for fear of a stronger son. From this act is born **Athena**, emerging fully armed from the skull of her father: strategy becomes the pillar of power.
The word **panic** comes from the god **Bang**. During a war against the Giants, his cry would have sowed sudden and irrational terror.

These myths do not make the gods models of virtue. They make mirrors of it: jealousy, fear of succession, thirst for reign. From Chaos to Olympus, the Greeks tell the story of how civilization attempts to master raw violence.
Greek mythology goes from **Chaos** to the order of **Olympus** through successive strokes of force. The gods share our passions, but not our mortality.
